paras: The Sibley's Mill shootings were a pair of fatal shootings in Baldwin County, Alabama, opposite Mobile, in late December 1881, in which a deputy sheriff and an unnamed Black man accused of ambushing the deputy's brother shot each other during an arrest. Deputy Sheriff Abe Johnson died within fifteen minutes, and a crowd that set out after the wounded suspect found him dead near a swamp. A Mobile dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, several of which presented the suspect's death as swift vengeance.

According to the Mobile dispatch, Joel Johnson, described as a well-known citizen of the neighborhood near Sibley's Mill, was riding along the public road when he was shot from behind a tree by a man the papers identified only as "a negro." Two papers dated the ambush to Monday, December 26. The dispatch said the attacker shot Johnson in the head, wrist and side, dragged him 300 yards into a pond, and rode off on his horse to a party in the neighborhood.

Johnson revived during the night and dragged himself half a mile home, where he told his brother Abe Johnson, a deputy sheriff, of the assault. His account, together with reports that the man had been seen on Joel Johnson's horse, led the deputy to set out to arrest him.

Abe Johnson found the suspect at the place of James Malone, called Jim Malone in most versions. In the fuller version of the dispatch, the man drew his pistol as the deputy made the arrest, the deputy shot him, and the man fired back, hitting Johnson in the breast, and ran. The deputy chased him a short way and fired again, then fell and died in fifteen minutes. The shorter version printed in Savannah said only that the man "resisted arrest" and "exchanged shots" with the deputy.

A crowd then gathered and went in search of the suspect. About 4 o'clock that afternoon they found him lying dead at the edge of a swamp, about half a mile down the creek, shot through the breast and wrist. A January digest stated that his death resulted from the shot Abe Johnson fired before he was killed, and no account reports the crowd firing on him.

The dead man's name was not printed in any of the coverage, and no report of an inquest appears in it. No report of Joel Johnson's death was found, although two January digests described him as "mortally wounded."

The story reached white papers through a Mobile telegram dated December 28 and ran the next day in New York, Chicago, Sacramento, Salt Lake City, St. Paul, Wheeling, Lancaster, Alexandria, Savannah, Dallas and Richmond. The New-York Tribune headed it "A Murder Quickly Avenged," the Savannah Morning News "A Brute Dispatched," and the Dallas Daily Herald "A Desperate Negro." The Wheeling Register's headline, "A Negro Murders Two White Men and is Then Shot," counted Joel Johnson among the dead, while the Chicago Tribune's deck spoke of "the Murder of an Officer, and the Death of the Criminal in a Swamp."

Shorter and increasingly garbled versions followed into January, including one Dakota paper that sent "Abe Johnson and brother and a deputy sheriff" in pursuit. Weekly crime digests in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa and Mississippi recast the suspect as "a negro horse thief" and "the black fiend." Every version presented the deputy's side of the encounter as fact, and none named the dead man or gave his account of the ambush.

The accounts differ over the suspect's wounds, given as the breast and wrist in most texts but the thigh and wrist in the Savannah Morning News. They also differ over whether Joel Johnson died: the fuller dispatches have him alive at home, while later digests call him mortally wounded.

reader.title: Sibley's Mill shootings
bases: The Black suspect was shot by Deputy Sheriff Abe Johnson while being arrested and was later found dead of the wound; no report has the searching crowd firing on him (A2, A19).
Every report goes back to one Mobile dispatch of December 28, carried in a long version (A2, A1) and a shorter one (A4, A10); no local Alabama paper, inquest or other independent account was found.

accounts.label: Mobile wire, long version
accounts.gist: The suspect drew his pistol as the deputy made the arrest; the deputy shot him, the suspect shot back and ran, and the deputy fired again before dying; a crowd later found the suspect dead.

accounts.label: Mobile wire, short version
accounts.gist: The suspect 'resisted arrest' and 'exchanged shots' with his pursuer, here a half brother of Joel; he escaped and was found dead half a mile away, shot through the thigh and wrist.

accounts.label: Weekly digests
accounts.gist: Condensed retellings say the suspect died of the shot the deputy fired before he was killed, and some call Joel 'mortally wounded'.

framing.detail: The New-York Tribune headed the dispatch 'A Murder Quickly Avenged' and the Savannah Morning News 'A Brute Dispatched'.
Most papers ran the Mobile wire unchanged under headings like 'Horrible Tragedy' or 'Double Tragedy in Alabama', calling the suspect 'the assassin'.
Weekly digests in January called the suspect 'a negro horse thief' and 'the black fiend'.
